newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to launch aluminium futures despite critics.
newsitem.headline: Japan to launch aluminium futures despite critics.

text.p: The Tokyo Commodity Exchange (TOCOM) is finally about to launch an aluminium futures contract, after countless delays over the past 10 years and despite industry opposition to the plan.
The yen-based aluminium futures contract, to begin trading on TOCOM on April 7, will be the first base metal futures contract in Japan.
"We've come a long way and believe the new contract will provide a risk hedging tool for Japan, which is a big consumer of aluminium," said a senior TOCOM official.
Japan imported 2.76 million tonnes of refined aluminium in calendar 1996, mainly from Brazil, Russia and Australia, Finance Ministry data showed.

Japan has been steadily forced to withdraw from domestic aluminium smelting since the early 1970s, when surging crude oil prices pushed up electricity costs sharply. Aluminium smelting is a highly electricity-intensive process.
In February, TOCOM approved 74 members to trade the new contract and 16 warehouses to store metal deliverable against the contracts in Japan.
The members include all nine of Japan's leading trade houses, as well as Engelhard Metals Japan Ltd, a subsidiary of U.S.-based Engelhard Corp.
The aluminium contract will be listed along with precious metal contracts on TOCOM's automated trading system.
TOCOM's first attempts to list an aluminium contract date back 10 years, when the exchange started inviting comments from local trade houses and studying overseas markets.
But it took much longer for the plan to bear fruit, mainly because of strong opposition from the local aluminium industry, industry officials said.

"Yes, we agree that it took longer then originally expected," said Naoaki Kurumada, director of the Trade Ministry's Commercial Affairs Office. "So we're now reviewing listing procedures for new contracts in the future."
The local aluminium industry has been vocal in its opposition to the new TOCOM contract.

"Japanese manufacturers depend on imported aluminium for about 100 percent of their consumption and currently use the London Metal Exchange (LME) to determine prices," Japan Aluminium Federation chairman Masahiro Kumamoto said in a statement.
"We'll request that TOCOM suspend trading if the new contract's price is very different from the LME and damages the physical market in Japan," Kumamoto said.
The ultimate goal of TOCOM is to become a Japanese version of the LME, listing other base metals and establishing a risk hedging market, industry officials said.

TOCOM president Naozo Mabuchi said in January the exchange plans to launch futures contracts for copper, lead and zinc within four to five years. But his ambitious ideas have already triggered controversy in the local metal industry.
Japan Mining Industry Association chairman Yumi Akimoto, who is also president of Mitsubishi Materials Corp, said this week he saw no need to list a copper futures contract in Japan.

Akimoto said the LME is effective in determining world prices and he expressed concern that speculators with no direct involvement in metals would wield influence over prices if copper futures were to be listed on TOCOM.
